ACCEPT `def:certified-handle`.

The correction is mathematically necessary and faithful. In the stated \(q_n\)-bit normalized radix-two model, the spacing in the binade \([1,2)\) is \(2^{1-q_n}\), so the former requirement that a bracketing enclosure have width at most \(2^{-q_n}\) can be impossible even for an ordinary nonrepresentable quantile in that binade. The replacement bound \(8\,2^{1-q_n}(1+|Q|)\) is a conservative mixed absolute/relative rounding bound and is attainable by directed rounding with arbitrary exponent range.

This does not weaken coverage, containment, or the statistical length claims: the returned interval must still contain the exact-real interval, and the actual quantile error remains recorded in \(\Delta_n^{\mathrm{arith}}\). The extra factor \(1+|Q|\) costs only \(O(\log(1+|Q|))\) additional precision bits and is compatible with polynomial precision schedules for the encoded normal and fixed-degree chi-square quantiles. Crucially, the deterministic certificate and implementation OEQ are not being declared solved by this edit; they remain obligations requiring the revised arithmetic radius to be propagated and proved negligible at the stated transition scales. Thus the change repairs an unrealizable implementation specification without introducing a loading assumption or laundering the research crux.
why: The construction correction replaces an unattainable pure absolute quantile-enclosure tolerance by an attainable mixed relative-plus-absolute directed-rounding bound while preserving exact-real containment, numerical-error accounting, and all statistical targets.

VERDICT:

1. `thm:deterministic-dyadic-certificate` statement change — ACCEPT.

The narrowing repairs a genuine information-model defect. A single nonrefinable interval does not specify one public control to arbitrary accuracy; it specifies a set of possible controls. For \(r=1\), \(F^{-1}_{\chi^2_2}(1-\gamma)=-2\log\gamma\), so an \(O(L)\)-bit interval permitting \(\gamma\in[2^{-2^L},1/4]\) has a quantile image of width \(\Theta(2^L)\). No algorithm receiving only that frozen interval can both cover every admissible quantile and meet the requested local relative-width bound. Requiring an exact dyadic value or a polynomial-time refinable certified name is therefore a legitimate specification of access to the public input, not a statistical or spectral assumption.

The REVIEW “assume-the-crux” warning does not apply substantively here. The new premise supplies progressively accurate enclosures of the input control only; it does not supply a quantile, an SVD, a gate decision, an endpoint enclosure, or a negligible-padding conclusion. Those remain outputs proved by the construction. The lane still separates deterministic exact-dyadic execution from encoding of the continuously distributed Gaussian observations.

2. `thm:certified-implementation` addition — ACCEPT.

The theorem is a result rather than a restatement of the desired certificate as a hypothesis. It gives explicit \(p_n,L_n,q_n\) schedules, bounds clipping probability, establishes a high-probability stable spectral box, invokes the newly proved stable-padding estimate to make every recorded numerical radius \(o(n^{-1})\) in expectation, and then transfers containment, coverage, transition length, and oracle length from \(I_n^{\mathrm{out}}\) to \(I_n^{\mathrm{fp}}\). The refinable-name premise is used only to obtain certified control intervals at the precision demanded by the quantile comparisons; it does not encode the construction’s crux.

Accordingly, both items preserve the original research claim under the minimally necessary correction that a real public control must be supplied as a value with effective precision access, rather than as a permanently ambiguous interval.
why: Independent review found the refinable-name premise to be a necessary input-representation condition rather than an assumption of the crux; the new theorem still constructs and proves the certified schedules, padding, containment, and statistical transfers.

The required material work is honest class positioning and completion of the certified-computation crux.

Class comparison: the note’s \(\mathcal P_n\) is not the full published Yan–Wainwright class. Their four-block theory permits rectangular blocks, formulates conditions through the full matrix’s donor-subblock conditioning and target-local incoherence, and does not impose this note’s square \(n\times n\) donor, fixed-rank ceiling, global donor incoherence, bounded-entry parameter space, or fixed one-row/one-column target geometry. See their four-block hypotheses (sub-block condition (4.2), noise condition (4.3), and local conditions (4.4a–c)) in arXiv:2401.13665v2.

The note is, however, an embedded canonical subclass. For the augmented matrix with blocks A,v,u,uA^+v, the span assumptions give rank r; take N1=T1=n and N2=T2=1. Strong spectrum and bounded u,v imply the anchor’s donor-subblock conditioning and bounded target leverage, while the constant entrywise Gaussian variance matches their normalization after setting their global noise parameter to order sigma n. Their (4.3) and (4.4a–b) then hold eventually, whereas (4.4c) fails at joint zero. Thus the upper result must be advertised as an extension in this square one-target subclass, not as a theorem over the entire published class. Upper coverage does not transfer from a subclass to the larger class. Conversely, thm:local-length-lower-bound does transfer upward: every procedure honest over the larger Yan–Wainwright class is honest on the embedded subclass, and the local alternatives used in the proof remain in that subclass.
